newsitem.title: GERMANY: German trade union leader hails ties with Greens.
newsitem.headline: German trade union leader hails ties with Greens.

text.p: The leader of Germany's trade unionists on Friday hailed progress in relations between his movement and the environmentalist Greens Party and said he hoped their cooperation would continue.

"Mutual trust has grown between us," Dieter Schulte told a Greens Party congress in the eastern town of Suhl. "We should continue to work on this without either of us placing too many demands on the other. We're ready to do that."
Schulte became the first head of the German Trade Union Federation (DGB), which has close ties to the main opposition Social Democrats (SPD), to speak to a Greens' congress.
"I think this is an expression of the normalisation of relations between us and this normalisation is the result of an increasingly open learning process on both sides," he said.

The Greens, who grew out of the peace movement and radical anti-capitalist protests of the 1960s and 1970s and only formally became a party 16 years ago, are now the third largest group in the German parliament.
"We now have more in common than just the belief that we have an incompotent government in Bonn," Schulte said.
The party hopes to use the three-day congress, which began with Schulte's speech on Friday evening, to portray itself as a responsible future partner in an SPD-led government.
In a boost to the leadership, members voted against changing the agenda to include a divisive debate on using military power as a last resort to resolve violent conflicts.

Pragmatists such as parliamentary co-leader Joschka Fischer returned from a fact-finding trip to Bosnia last month strengthened in their conviction that German troops should take part in the next international peace mission to the Balkans.
But idealists passionately committed to the party's pacifist origins insist Germany's Nazi past means it should not carry out military missions on foreign soil.
Many leading figures in the party had said they would rather avoid the topic, which provoked a bitter debate at last year's conference in Bremen, at the Suhl congress.
Officials want to concentrate on convincing voters the party is capable of being more than just the country's environmental conscience.
A range of economic policies is on the agenda, including a radical plan to slash the basic rate of income tax.
The congress got off to a shaky start as many delegates, including party co-leader Jeurgen Trittin, arrived more than an hour late as public transport ground to a haltin heavy snow.
